title: Studying with Andrew Jacobson in Boston
summary: Milt remembers waiting while Thomas took lessons with Jacobson, who taught relaxing the tongue on attack; Thomas explains how he found him through Henry Williams.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: You were studying with Merle Johnson.
Now, who was that man that I used to see you study with in Boston?
Jacobson. Across from Symphony Hall, right?
Remember me going up with you?
I loved you ...(?)., I followed you everywhere, man.
Because you were my ideal, man. You were (?) the most perfect (?)...

That guy showed me the secret... Now, I had studied from Merle. I used to get mad, man. Merle used to beat you on the back to make you relax. But Jacobson said, "All you got to do when you make your attack is let your tongue relax." He says, because the tongue goes down in your throat, and if you tighten it up here, it tightens up in your throat. And he said "The throat ain't but so big, so you got to let it go."

See, how I got to Jacobson... There was a guy in New York named Henry Williams(?), and I had heard him play, boy, and he had the most gorgeous tone I'd heard on saxophone. And I heard...I don't know... I was checking some of the New York scene. I found out that he'd studied from a guy in Boston named Jacobson. And we was always going to Boston. So the next time I went to Boston, I looked up Jacobson, made an appointment with him on Friday, took my first lesson -- and boy, he shook me up so much and showed me so much that first lesson... See, I was an advanced musician. I just wasn't no beginner then. So right when I got through with that lesson, I made an appointment for him to take a lesson on Monday. Because I wanted to try to get... I was only going to be in town a week, so I wanted to get as much out of him as I could. I took this lesson on Monday, and I made another appointment for Thursday. Because all I had to do was practice, and he knew how I was about practicing. I could practice that stuff and have it... Because he showed me how to take the water off the reed...
And he told me that he invented subtones, and I kind of I halfway believed him. Because he played subtones on clarinet, alto, anything he picked up...
